title: The One God Who Spoke Openly
english: …should we offer up songs of thanksgiving? “I am, then, and there is no other” (Isaiah 45:18). For if He it is who made the heaven, who showed forth the earth and did not make it for nothing but to be inhabited, who else could be thought to be God besides Him? Or who could equal Him in strength and glory? Or who could come near Him at all, even by a little? And how is the whole nature of created things not surpassed by a glory, strength and wisdom so great and so far above all things? There is no one. He alone, then, and no other at all besides Him, could be thought to be God by nature and in truth.

Yes, but someone might perhaps say: “Who has known His purpose in this? Or who can tell whether He wishes some others also to be crowned with the glory and the name of God, or Himself alone?” So He answers this and says: “I have not spoken in secret, nor in a dark place of the earth; I did not say to the offspring of Jacob, ‘Seek vain things’” (Isaiah 45:19). I laid down laws for them about these things, He says, not speaking in a corner or trying to escape notice, but clearly and openly.

For the Lord came down on Mount Sinai in the form of fire; there was darkness and storm and smoke, and the piercing sound of trumpets (Exodus 19:16-19; Hebrews 12:18-19). The whole people stood by, with Moses acting as mediator, and laws were proclaimed from God. He did not charge Israel to seek anything vain, that is, an idol or a falsely named object of worship; on the contrary, the commandments kept them from such things. For it was said to him: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him alone shall you serve (Matthew 4:10; Deuteronomy 6:13); and you shall have no other gods besides Me. And you shall not make for yourself an idol, nor the likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or on the earth below, or in the waters under the earth” (Exodus 20:3-4).

So it was said to him. And the words “I am the Lord” are as if He were saying, not once but many times over, “I alone am God and Lord of all, speaking righteousness and declaring truth” (Isaiah 45:19). By righteousness, I think, He means the Law, for the Law is the arbiter of righteousness; and by truth, the teachings of Christ. Yet the outline of the truth is present in the Law (Romans 2:20), and the mystery of Christ lies hidden in its shadows; for Moses wrote about Him (John 5:46). So in speaking righteousness, the power of the truth is also declared along with it, since it is true that the Law was a shadow (Hebrews 10:1), and that in it now lies the outline of the truth.

“Gather together and come, take counsel together, you who are being saved from the nations. Those who carry the wood, their carved image, did not know, and they pray as to gods that do not save” (Isaiah 45:20).

title: The Bird from the East
english: But if the God of all wishes to do anything, what could there be to stand against it and oppose it? For “what the holy God wills, who will scatter? And His high hand, who will turn it back?” (Isaiah 14:27). So, as proof that He is God by nature and in truth, He may fittingly say: “All My counsel will stand, and all that I have planned I will do” (Isaiah 46:10). Then He adds to this: “calling a bird from the east, and from a land far off, for the things I have planned” (Isaiah 46:11); and to this also the words “I am” will be joined.

The bird called from the east and from a land far off we say is the Babylonian, who set fire to the whole country of the Jews, took Jerusalem and shook down the temple in it. Then, uprooting very many of both the common people and the notable, he carried them away from their native land and settled them in the country and land of the Persians, laying on them the hard and unbearable yoke of captivity. This too will be clear to you from what God said to the blessed prophet Ezekiel. It runs thus:

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, tell a tale and speak a parable to the house of Israel, and say: Thus says Adonai, the Lord: The great eagle, of great span, full of talons, whose purpose is to enter Lebanon, took the choice parts of the cedar; he nipped off the tops of its tender shoots and brought them into the land of Canaan; he set them in a walled city. And he took some of the seed of the land and put it in the plain as a plant beside much water; he set it where it could be watched over. And it became a weak vine, small in size, so that its branches showed toward him, and its roots were beneath it in its ground. And it became a vine, and put out shoots, and stretched out its climbing branches” (Ezekiel 17:1-6).

These things God said to the blessed prophet Ezekiel. But since the saying was hard to grasp and the force of its meaning not very clear to the hearers, He Himself explains it again, saying: “Say to the rebellious house of Israel: Do you not know what these things are that I have said? When the king of Babylon comes against Jerusalem, he will take its king and its rulers and lead them to himself into Babylon. And he will take one of the royal seed, and make a covenant with him, and bring him under a curse; and he will take the leaders of the land, so that the kingdom may become weak and never lift itself up, but keep his covenant and uphold it” (Ezekiel 17:12-14).

title: God’s Forbearance toward a Hard People
english: …temple, when the ministering priests sang of Jerusalem: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God” (Psalm 87:3). The Lord Himself also recalls this, when He says that no one should swear by his own head, because he cannot make one hair white or black, nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King (Matthew 5:35-36). For they used to swear by Jerusalem, calling it, as I said, the city of God. And they leaned on Him too, saying that the Lord of hosts was their strength (compare Isaiah 48:2).

But those who then held this belief ought not to have profaned the city of God with altars and sacrifices, entangled as they were in the deceits of demons, nor to have provoked against themselves the One in whom they trusted; rather they should have gladdened Him with good pursuits, bringing Him, like a sacrifice, a steadfast devotion.

Yet “hear these things,” He says (Isaiah 48:1). And what are they? “The former things I declared long ago; they went out of my mouth and were made known. Suddenly I did them, and they came to pass” (Isaiah 48:3). For, as I said, in the beginning Manasseh, hateful to God, gathered from everywhere the so-called diviners and augurs (compare 2 Kings 21:6) and was always prying into the future; carried away by their charlatan tricks, he perhaps thought that he knew it clearly. That is why the God of all says: It was I who declared to you the first things too; these were not spoken to you by any other of the falsely named gods, but went out of My mouth; it was made known to you, and suddenly I did it, and it came. That is, even if you did not expect these things to come to fulfillment, still you learned through the events themselves and by actual experience that I both did it and it came.

He seems to call “former” the misery brought on them by the war, when they were carried off from their native land, took up the yoke of bitter slavery, and were taken away into the country of the Persians and Medes. For it was second, after those events, that the things brought on the Babylonians by divine wrath befell them, which we have already described at great length.
“I know that you are hard, and your neck is an iron sinew, and your forehead bronze. And I declared to you of old, before it came upon you; I made it known to you” (Isaiah 48:4-5).

Here he shows the incomparable gentleness of the supreme nature, and how great the mercy it shows to human beings, even to those who are used to grieving Him deeply. For its calm forbearance matches its own glory. And just as by boundless excellence it rises far above the measure of created things, so too it is beyond comparison in its love for humankind.
